english: Let $C$ be the parabola $y^{2}=12x$ and let $E$ be the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{\alpha^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{16}=1$, where $\alpha>4$. Suppose that there is a point $Q$ on $E$ such that the tangent to $E$ at $Q$ and the normal to $E$ at $Q$ both touch $C$. Then the eccentricity of $E$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $C$ परवलय $y^{2}=12x$ है तथा $E$ दीर्घवृत्त $\dfrac{x^{2}}{\alpha^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{16}=1$ है, जहाँ $\alpha>4$ है। माना कि $E$ पर एक बिन्दु $Q$ ऐसा है कि $Q$ पर $E$ की स्पर्श रेखा तथा $Q$ पर $E$ का अभिलम्ब, दोनों $C$ को स्पर्श करते हैं। तब $E$ की उत्केन्द्रता ______ है।
solution: The tangent and normal at $Q$ are perpendicular lines through $Q$, both tangent to $C$; perpendicular tangents of a parabola meet on its directrix, so $Q$ lies on $x=-3$: $Q(-3,k)$, $k\neq0$

$e=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{16}{25}}=\dfrac{3}{5}$ (then $Q=\left(-3,\pm\dfrac{16}{5}\right)$, an end of a latus rectum of $E$; the normal there, of slope $-\dfrac{5}{3}$ and intercept $-\dfrac{9}{5}$, also satisfies $c=\dfrac{3}{m}$)
solution_full: The tangent and the normal to $E$ at $Q$ are two perpendicular lines through $Q$. Both touch $C$, so $Q$ is a point from which two perpendicular tangents can be drawn to $C$. The locus of such points (the director circle of a parabola) is its directrix, here $x=-3$.
So $Q=(-3,k)$. If $k=0$, $Q=(-3,0)$ would need $\alpha=3$, contrary to $\alpha>4$; hence $k\neq0$, and the tangent to $E$ at $Q$ is not vertical.
Tangent to $E$ at $Q$: $\dfrac{-3x}{\alpha^{2}}+\dfrac{ky}{16}=1$, i.e. $y=\dfrac{48}{\alpha^{2}k}x+\dfrac{16}{k}$: slope $m=\dfrac{48}{\alpha^{2}k}$, intercept $c=\dfrac{16}{k}$.
For $y^{2}=12x$ ($a=3$) the line $y=mx+c$ is a tangent iff $c=\dfrac{3}{m}$: $\dfrac{16}{k}=\dfrac{3\alpha^{2}k}{48}=\dfrac{\alpha^{2}k}{16}$, so $k^{2}=\dfrac{256}{\alpha^{2}}$.

Check the normal: at $Q\left(-3,\dfrac{16}{5}\right)$ the tangent has slope $\dfrac{48}{25\cdot\frac{16}{5}}=\dfrac{3}{5}$, so the normal is $y-\dfrac{16}{5}=-\dfrac{5}{3}(x+3)$, i.e. $y=-\dfrac{5}{3}x-\dfrac{9}{5}$; and $\dfrac{3}{m}=\dfrac{3}{-5/3}=-\dfrac{9}{5}$, so it touches $C$ too.
Eccentricity of $E$: $e=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{16}{25}}=\dfrac{3}{5}=0.6$. (The foci of $E$ are $(\pm3,0)$, so $x=-3$ is the latus-rectum line of $E$ and $Q$ is an end of the latus rectum.)
originality_note: New: a point of an ellipse whose tangent and normal both touch a parabola must lie on the parabola's directrix, which forces the directrix to be a latus-rectum line of the ellipse (way 4, hidden invariant). Closest known: 'the tangent to y^2 = 4x at (t^2, 2t) is the normal to 4x^2 + 5y^2 = 20 at a given point' (a published problem) and common tangents of an ellipse and a parabola. Different because: both the tangent and the normal at the same point must touch the parabola, and the key step is the perpendicular-tangents locus, not a slope equation.

concept_use.Tangent to the parabola: point, slope an: The tangency condition c = a/m for y^2 = 12x is applied to the ellipse's tangent at Q, and perpendicular tangents of the parabola are used to place Q on the directrix.
concept_use.Tangent and normal for Ellipse: The tangent to E at Q(-3, k) is written as -3x/alpha^2 + ky/16 = 1, and the normal at Q is checked to touch C as well.

stem_review: Read as a student: every curve and point is defined before use, every condition is stated, each sentence has one reading; the answer was recomputed with sympy and checked by an independent numerical route, is unique and matches the Answer Plan; no hyperbolic functions or asymptotes. Checked that the configuration exists and is unique for alpha > 4 (sympy finds only alpha = 5), that the excluded case k = 0 cannot occur, and that 0.60 is a decimal between 0 and 1 as planned. Changed: the first design (a line tangent to the parabola and normal to an ellipse, asking its slope) was replaced after the web check found a published problem with the same core.
key_step: Seeing that a tangent and a normal at the same point are perpendicular tangents of the parabola, so the point lies on its directrix.
justification: Two linked ideas (perpendicular tangents meet on the directrix; tangency condition c = a/m) give a short route, but the first idea is not prompted, and direct algebra without it is long; numerical answer. Comparable to the ellipse-parabola tangent anchor 2023-P1-Q2 (L3).
